title: Meeting J. D. on Hilliard Street
summary: The boys ask J. D. what he plays, and J. D. sings a monkey song.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: said, 'Oh, yeah, he's very nice. I met him, you know, say -- all the children knew he was over on the stage, you see, and that was -- there was kind of happiness with him. They was kind of proud of him, you see. And that part of the city was known as Fourth Ward in Atlanta, Georgia.

And so eventually one day we was talking about him, and he happened to come up the street by himself, Hilliard Street, you see, and (inaudible) and (inaudible), 'Oh, here comes J. D., you know. I think it was John Peters that said it, 'Here come J. D. Said, 'What you going to say to him? Let's talk to -- let's ask him something, you know. Let's ask him about could he teach or help Boodjie with his -- teach Boodjie some tap dancing,' because my cousin was sitting there, first cousin, my Aunt Mary's son, Boby, you see, Boby Green. His name was James also, you see.

So sure enough, J. D. turned out to be a lovable person, you know. He had to be lovable, a little boy like that walking his mother, you know, and he was actually like a little man, you see. And he was very nice. So he set down with us. 'What you all -- what you fellows -- what you -- what are you all doing?' you know?

Right -- what have you been playing, you know? So we said something, well, we used to shoot marbles, you know. We was tossing bottle tops and so on and so on and so on. And they called it lag, you know, what you call pitching the
pennies, coins to the curb and stuff like that.

And he had a little song he used to sing, 'oh, the monkey wrapped his tail around the flagpole, showed his flagpole to the crowd, you know. And, you know, he was a cute little fellow, you see. Well, we all, we get to be friends easily. Children always do, right?
